report.source_text: Cone beam computed tomography was performed for a more detailed assessment. Figure 2a and b show an expansive mass affecting the posterior region of the right maxilla, extending to the base of the maxillary sinus. The lesion shows heterogeneous areas with varying density, suggesting mixed lytic and sclerotic components, characteristic of aggressive lesions. The presence of bone destruction is evident, with compromised bone margins and involvement of adjacent structures, indicating invasive behavior of the mass. The mass is also visible in Fig. 2c and d, causing alterations to the bone contour and invading adjacent tissues. Significant erosion of the right maxillary bone can be seen, with areas of mixed density. The irregular density of the tumor suggests the production of osteoid matrix. The extension of the lesion beyond the primary bone structures reinforces the aggressive and infiltrative nature of the lesion.

report.source_text: The absence of nuclear expression suggests that the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway is not activated in this tumor, a relevant feature since nuclear translocation of beta-catenin is associated with certain types of neoplasms where this pathway is activated. Expression restricted to the cytoplasm also indicates that the tumor has histological characteristics that differentiate it from neoplasms in which nuclear beta-catenin plays a significant role in biological behavior. The CD34 marker showed prominent positive immunoreactivity in the endothelial cells lining the blood vessels in the tumor stroma. The presence of CD34 in blood vessels makes it possible to visualize the intratumoral vascular architecture, which shows a pattern of vascularization characteristic of tumours with high angiogenesis. The absence of staining in tumor cells indicates that this marker is limited to the vascular endothelium and does not suggest hematopoietic differentiation or other origins for the tumor. Ki-67 expression (Fig. 3) is markedly positive in a large number of cells, reflecting a high rate of cellular disruption in the tumor. This intense nuclear labeling is indicative of high mitotic activity, a common feature in high-grade neoplasms. The three slides confirmed the widespread presence of Ki-67, with a high proportion of marked cells, indicating that the tumor has a potential for aggressive and rapid growth. This marker therefore reinforces the tumor’s intense proliferative behavior. Desmin staining shows no immunoreactivity in the tumor cells, underlining the absence of muscle differentiation. Negativity for desmin indicates that the tumor is not related to smooth or skeletal muscle tissues, helping to exclude neoplasms such as leiomyosarcomas and rhabdomyosarcomas. Investigation for myogenin, a specific marker for skeletal muscle differentiation, showed no immunoreactivity in the tumor cells, highlighting the absence of differentiation to skeletal muscle. This absence is important for differential diagnosis, as neoplasms such as rhabdomyosarcoma would be positive for myogenin. The negativity of the tumor for this marker indicates that it does not have histological characteristics of muscle differentiation. Testing for pancytokeratin, a marker of epithelial differentiation, was negative in tumor cells. The absence of reactivity for cytokeratin suggests that the tumor does not have an epithelial origin, which helps to exclude carcinomas and other epithelium-derived tumors. Negativity for this marker indicates that the tumor cells did not have epithelial characteristics, reinforcing the hypothesis of a mesenchymal or non-epithelial tumor. Staining for smooth muscle actin (U70) showed no immunoreactivity in the tumor cells, indicating that the tumor does not show smooth muscle differentiation. The absence of muscle actin in the cells reinforces that the tumor does not have myoid characteristics, such as those seen in leiomyosarcomas or other smooth muscle tumors. This negativity is essential to avoid tumors with a muscular origin or differentiation.

report.source_text: After performing the incisional biopsy, which resulted in an initial analysis of the nature of the tumor and confirmation of the pathological entity, the definitive surgical procedures were planned and performed. The aim of this surgical approach was complete resection of the lesion, taking into account the extent of tumor invasion identified on imaging tests and confirmed by histopathological findings. The procedure included careful removal of the compromised tumor tissue, with a safety margin to reduce the risk of local recurrence (Fig. 4a and b), accompanied by removal of the affected area to restore functionality and aesthetics to the maxillofacial region. The surgical specimen was sent for further histopathological analysis (Fig. 4c).

report.source_text: The slides stained with hematoxylin and eosin (HE) (Fig. 6) show the classic characteristics of a small cell osteosarcoma lesion, as evidenced by the cellular and stromal pattern. There is an intense proliferation of small, round cells with a monotonous appearance, distributed in a dense and disorganized manner. These cells have a hyperchromatic nucleus and scarce cytoplasm, reinforcing the undifferentiated nature of the neoplasm. In addition, there are areas where the stroma is mineralized, with the presence of irregularly arranged bone matrix formation, a fundamental feature for the diagnosis of osteosarcoma, as it indicates direct production of osteoid matrix by the tumour cells. Another notable feature is the infiltrative aspect of the lesion, with tumor cells invading and breaking through the adjacent tissue architecture, without defined boundaries.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Small cell osteosarcoma of the right maxilla
clinician.trajectory_summary: An 8-year-old female presented with progressive edema in the right maxillofacial region over approximately one month, initially asymptomatic then developing local discomfort and difficulty chewing. Clinical examination revealed significant facial asymmetry with bulging in the right maxillary region, pronounced intraoral swelling in the posterior right maxilla with smooth surface, erythema, hard palate expansion, and mucosal hyperemia, suggesting an underlying expansive process. Cone beam computed tomography demonstrated an expansive mass in the posterior right maxilla extending to the maxillary sinus base with heterogeneous mixed lytic and sclerotic density pattern, bone destruction with compromised margins, invasion of adjacent structures, and irregular density suggesting osteoid matrix production. An incisional biopsy was performed due to clinical and radiographic suspicion of malignancy. Immunohistochemistry showed high Ki-67 positivity indicating high mitotic activity and aggressive behavior, CD34 positivity in vascular endothelium indicating high angiogenesis, and negativity for desmin, myogenin, pan-cytokeratin, and U70, excluding muscle and epithelial differentiation and supporting mesenchymal origin. Definitive surgical resection with safety margins was performed. Surgical specimen histopathology confirmed the diagnosis of small cell osteosarcoma, characterized by intense proliferation of small round hyperchromatic cells with scarce cytoplasm in a dense disorganized pattern, mineralized stroma with irregularly arranged bone matrix formation indicating direct osteoid production by tumor cells, and infiltrative aspect with tumor cells invading adjacent tissue without defined boundaries.
